extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science; scientifically-minded readers learning methods of inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and methodological guidance on how scientific laws are discovered, verified, and explained — including the Deductive Method (Induction, Ratiocination, Verification) and three modes of resolving laws into other laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method components
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method consists of three constituent parts: Induction, Ratiocination (deduction), and Verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three parts are essential; without Verification the results of deduction remain little more than conjecture. The text repeatedly treats these three as jointly necessary for reliable deductive science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: empirical agreement required
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance on conclusions arrived at by deduction, these conclusions must be found, on careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experience confirms deductive conclusions in known cases, we may trust them in other cases; if not, the theory is imperfect. Verification is the test that distinguishes conjecture from trustworthy theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification must explain discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: If deductions predict an effect from a combination of causes, then in known cases where that combination existed but the effect did not follow, the theory must show (or make a probable surmise) what frustrated it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to account for counterexamples indicates the theory is imperfect. Verification is incomplete unless such discrepancies can be explained or plausibly surmised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification completeness: use comparable complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification is not complete unless some of the cases in which the theory is borne out are of at least equal complexity with any other cases in which its application could be called for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A theory should be confirmed by instances as complex as those to which it will be applied; simple confirmations are insufficient when the target cases are complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best verification: theory deduces empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effectual verification of a theory is that it leads deductively to the empirical laws of the phenomena (whether these are universally true or only generally true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If observed uniformities are accounted for as necessary consequences of the proposed causes, this strongly confirms the theory (example: Newtonian theory leading to Kepler's laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex cases can serve as verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex instances that could not help discover a simple law may nevertheless, when consistent with that law, become additional evidence supporting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex case agreeing with a theory functions as a new experiment in different circumstances and can eliminate previously unexcluded circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as deriving one law from others
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature is explained when other law(s) are pointed out of which that law is a case and from which it can be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation here is philosophical: substituting a more general law (often less familiar) for a particular one; it does not provide an ultimate 'why' but shows how the partial law follows from more general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode 1 — Composition of causes (resolution into separate causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex law (effect of combined causes) is explained by resolving it into the separate laws of the causes which contribute to it, together with the fact of their co-existence (collocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: planetary motion resolved into law of rectilineal motion and law of centripetal force plus the existence and relative amounts of those forces. Both the laws and the collocation are essential elements of the explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collocations as essential explanatory elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations of complex effects require not only laws of separate causes but the collocations — the existence of certain agents or powers in certain circumstances of place and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collocations (who/what is present and in what proportion) are an integral part of resolving complex laws; omitting them leaves the resolution incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode 2 — Intermediate links (proximate vs remote causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When further observation detects an intermediate link, the sequence A → C is resolved into A → B and B → C, so that the original A is a remote cause acting through B the proximate cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode clarifies that apparent direct causal sequences may hide intervening phenomena (examples: touch → nerve-affection → sensation; acid → separation of elements → charring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolved laws are more general and more reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law is resolved into other laws (by either mode), the latter are laws more general than the original, and, typically, more to be relied on (less likely to require limitation by subsequent experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the more immediate laws have fewer contingent negative conditions, they hold under more circumstances and are less liable to failure than the complex derived law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex laws are less general and more failure-prone
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a complex effect is less general and more subject to failure than the laws of any single cause composing it, since it is defeated by any contingency that defeats any component law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: prefer explanations in terms of simpler component laws; be cautious applying complex joint-effect laws universally. Small defects (e.g., rust) can prevent expected joint effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to proportions: qualitative changes from quantitative variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when causes obey the same simple laws, differences in the proportions in which they combine can produce qualitatively different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: varying the ratio of centripetal to tangent force can change planetary motion from ellipse to circle, parabola, or hyperbola. Thus explanation must consider not only presence but relative magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode 3 — Subsumption under a more general law
rubrics_metrics.description: Several partial laws may be gathered under one more general law which includes them all (subsumption); general laws are often arrived at by showing that similar phenomena conform quantitatively as well as qualitatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: terrestrial gravity and planetary centripetal tendencies were subsumed under universal gravitation by demonstrating quantitative identity in corresponding circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: General laws arise by combining partial laws from diverse instances
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach very general laws often requires many distinct sets of experiments or observations, at different times and by different people; one set shows the law under some conditions, another under others, and combined they indicate a more general law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general law is effectively the sum of the partial ones; assembling observations that eliminate particular circumstances yields broader laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of circumstances to generalize laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization requires eliminating particular circumstances (e.g., proximity to Earth) by finding classes of instances where those circumstances differ, thereby revealing the common underlying law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: celestial observations eliminated terrestrial proximity, showing gravity is not a property of the Earth alone. Seek observations across varying conditions to test universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation does not equal causal 'accounting' beyond laws and collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: To say a law is 'accounted for' means no more than assigning other, more general laws together with collocations from which the partial law follows; it is incorrect to treat the general law as the cause of the partial law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate a general law being a case with the general law being the cause of its instances. Explanation replaces mystery with a possibly more general (not necessarily more familiar) mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific aim: minimize assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole problem of the investigation of nature is to find the fewest general propositions whose grant would make the order of nature as it exists the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological implication: prefer theories that reduce the number of independent assumptions needed to deduce observed uniformities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological tools: Method of Agreement and comprehensive description
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate verification and discovery, ascertain empirical laws by comparing instances conformably to the Method of Agreement and describe phenomena comprehensively and accurately, collecting simple expressions for wholes from observations of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express observed series in progressively simpler correct forms (e.g., circle → epicycles → ellipse) and use agreement across instances to establish empirical regularities usable for deductive verification.
